Herem
HEH-rem (Hebrew ḥ as in Scottish “loch”)
n. (Hebrew; Old Testament holy war and consecration law)
From Hebrew ḥērem (חֵרֶם), the devoted thing or ban; root ḥ-r-m carries the sense of prohibition and sacred separation. The verb ḥāram means to devote to destruction, to place under the ban. Cognate with Arabic ḥaram (forbidden, sacred space). The Septuagint renders ḥērem as anathema, which the New Testament inherits.

Biblical Definition

Hērem (Hebrew: חֵרֶם, “the ban,” “devoted thing”) is the sacred act of placing persons, cities, or property under irrevocable consecration to the LORD — either for His exclusive possession or for total destruction as an act of holy judgment. What is devoted under ḥērem cannot be redeemed or sold but belongs absolutely to God. Leviticus 27:28 distinguishes the ḥērem from ordinary vows: “every devoted offering is most holy to the LORD.” In the conquest narratives, the LORD commanded Israel to place Canaanite cities under ḥērem: Jericho was “doomed by the LORD to destruction” (Josh 6:17); Israel vowed, “And Israel vowed a vow unto the LORD, and said, If thou wilt indeed deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities.” (Num 21:2). The theological logic is precise: Canaan's inhabitants were ripe for judgment after four hundred years of wickedness (Gen 15:16); Israel was not a superior nation claiming conquest by merit but the instrument of divine judicial execution against covenant-breaking peoples. Achan's sin (Josh 7) illustrates the severity: taking from the ḥērem extended the ban to the taker, for what belongs to the LORD cannot be privately appropriated. The New Testament antitype is inescapable: anathema (the Greek rendering of ḥērem) carries the same sense of irrevocable divine exclusion (1 Cor 16:22; Gal 1:8-9). The ḥērem reveals that divine holiness cannot coexist with unremediated sin; only the greater Joshua — Christ Himself, who bore the curse of the ḥērem for His people (Gal 3:13) — brings them safely through the ban.

Webster 1828 Definition

The Hebrew term for the “devoted thing” or “ban” in Old Testament law and holy war: persons, cities, or property irrevocably consecrated to the LORD — either for His exclusive use or for total destruction as an act of holy judgment from which no redemption is possible.

HEREM, n. (Hebrew ḥērem, חֵרֶם). The sacred ban in Old Testament law and holy war; that which is irrevocably devoted to the LORD, placed beyond human disposal — either consecrated property belonging to God alone, or condemned persons and cities given over to total destruction.

The concept divides into two aspects: positive ḥērem (devotion of valuable things to the sanctuary, as in Lev 27:28) and negative ḥērem (the war ban commanding total destruction of enemies, as in Deut 7:2 and Josh 6:17). Both share the logic of irrevocable divine claim: what is devoted cannot be retrieved for human use.

The Septuagint translates ḥērem as anathema, which the New Testament inherits. Paul pronounces anathema on any gospel-perverter (Gal 1:8-9) and on those who do not love the Lord (1 Cor 16:22), reflecting the same logic of irrevocable divine exclusion applied now to apostasy from the gospel.

Critical scholarship and progressive evangelical ethics condemn the ḥērem passages as evidence of a morally primitive tribal religion. This misreads both Testaments: the conquest's ḥērem was judicial execution of covenant-breaking peoples after four centuries of wickedness (Gen 15:16), not genocide for tribal advantage. Israel itself was not exempt: apostate Israelite cities underwent the same ban (Deut 13:15-16).

The theological weight of ḥērem is Christological: Christ bore the curse of the law (Gal 3:13), absorbing the ban that fallen humanity deserved, so that His people are rescued from the judgment it represents. The cross is the ultimate ḥērem — the definitive act in which God's holy claim on sinners is satisfied by the one righteous Substitute who willingly went under the ban for them.

Key Scripture

Deuteronomy 7:2 — "And when the LORD thy God shall deliver them before thee; thou shalt smite them, and utterly destroy them; thou shalt make no covenant with them, nor shew mercy unto them:"

Joshua 6:17 — "And the city shall be accursed, even it, and all that are therein, to the LORD: only Rahab the harlot shall live, she and all that are with her in the house, because she hid the messengers that we sent."

Leviticus 27:28 — "Notwithstanding no devoted thing, that a man shall devote unto the LORD of all that he hath, both of man and beast, and of the field of his possession, shall be sold or redeemed: every devoted thing is most holy unto the LORD."

Numbers 21:2 — "And Israel vowed a vow unto the LORD, and said, If thou wilt indeed deliver this people into my hand, then I will utterly destroy their cities."

Modern Corruption

Modern critical scholarship and progressive evangelical ethics condemn the ḥērem as morally primitive or genocidal, evacuating its theological logic; revisionist interpreters deny the historicity of the conquest to sidestep the text's moral weight.

expand to see more

Progressive evangelical and liberal-Protestant readings of ḥērem treat the conquest passages as sub-Christian testimony that the New Testament corrects or transcends — an embarrassment to be explained away by “evolutionary revelation” or accommodation theology. Eric Seibert, Peter Enns, and others argue that Scripture's portrayal of a commanding God is ancient Israelite theological projection, not reliable revelation about God's actual character. This position abandons biblical inerrancy in favor of a canon-within-the-canon constructed on progressive-ethical grounds, making the interpreter rather than Scripture the judge of which divine commands are authentic. It is not a humble correction of theological crudeness; it is a systematic rejection of the God who actually revealed Himself in both Testaments.

The moral objection to ḥērem ignores that the Canaanite peoples' judgment was neither arbitrary nor racially motivated. Genesis 15:16 reveals that the iniquity of the Amorites was “not yet complete” in Abraham's day, meaning four centuries of accumulated covenant-breaking wickedness preceded the conquest judgment. Israel itself was not immune from the ban's logic: the same destruction fell on apostate Israelite cities (Deut 13:15-16) and ultimately on Jerusalem in 586 BC and AD 70. The ḥērem is not ethnic cleansing; it is theocratic capital punishment on a national scale, carried out by the God whose holiness is absolute, whose patience is long, and whose justice is finally inexorable.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

From Hebrew ḥērem (חֵרֶם), root ḥ-r-m; cognate with Arabic ḥaram (forbidden, sacred); the Septuagint renders it as Greek anathema, carrying the force into the New Testament's vocabulary of irrevocable divine exclusion.

expand to see more

Hebrew ḥērem (חֵרֶם) — devoted thing, ban; root ḥ-r-m carries the sense of prohibition and sacred separation; cognate with Arabic ḥaram (forbidden, sacred space), the root behind “harem” (forbidden enclosure) in Arabic usage.

Hebrew verb ḥāram (חָרַם) — to devote to destruction, to place under the ban; the Hiphil stem emphasizes the completed act of total destruction; regularly rendered “utterly destroy” in English translations of Deuteronomy and Joshua.

Greek anathema (ἀνάθεμα) — the Septuagint's translation of ḥērem; a thing dedicated to divinity and therefore removed from common use, either for consecration or for destruction; Paul employs it for gospel-perverters (Gal 1:8-9) and Lord-rejecters (1 Cor 16:22).

Greek katara (κατάρα) — curse; Gal 3:13 (“Christ redeemed us from the curse of the Law”) uses katara for the covenantal ban that Christ absorbed; this is the Christological resolution of ḥērem — the Righteous One placed Himself under the curse reserved for the covenant-breakers.

Latin devotio — the Roman parallel concept: the ritual devotion of an enemy leader to the underworld gods for destruction; a pagan echo of the same logic of irrevocable divine claim over what is consecrated to judgment, stripped of its covenantal and redemptive content.

Usage

"The ḥērem cannot be assigned to the “Old Testament God” as if He were morally different from the New Testament Father; both Testaments present the same holy God whose judgment on sin is certain and severe, and whose mercy is received only on His own terms."

"The seriousness with which Israel treated the ban — and the communal catastrophe of Achan's violation — is a pastoral word to the church: presumptuous sin in the covenant community carries communal consequences that cheap-grace teaching consistently ignores."

"The ban's Christological resolution — Christ bearing the curse so that His people escape it — is what makes holy-war ethics intelligible across the canon: the final enemy is not a Canaanite tribe but sin and death themselves, and the greater Joshua defeats them at Golgotha."
